For any  $\ell=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{m})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}$ , let  $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\subset L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma})$  be the space of operators  $X$  such that  $\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}<+\infty$  and for any  $n=(n_{1},\dots,n_{m})$
their matrix entries in the Fock basis satisfy
$\langle n_{1},\dots,n_{m}|X|n_{1}+\ell^{\prime}_{1},\dots,n_{m}+\ell^{\prime}_{m}\rangle=0,\qquad\forall\ell^{\prime}\neq\ell.$
Then, any operator  $X$  with  $\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}<+\infty$  can be decomposed as
$\displaystyle X=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}}X_{\ell},\qquad\quad X_{\ell}\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}.$
(40)
Following [6] we call (40) the diagonal decomposition of  $X$ . A crucial property of the diagonal decomposition is that  $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ ’s are orthogonal subspaces, and  $\langle X_{\ell},X_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}=0$  if  $\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}$ . This is a consequence of the fact that  $\widehat{\sigma}$  is diagonal in the Fock basis.
Corollary 8.
[9]
For any  $\ell\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}$  the subspace  $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$  is invariant under  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}$ , and the eigenvalues of  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}$  restricted to  $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$  are contained in  $\big\{\sum_{j}\sinh(\beta_{j}/2)k_{j}:~k_{j}\geq|\ell_{j}|\big\}$ . In particular, for any  $X_{\ell}\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$  we have
$\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sinh(\beta_{j}/2)|\ell_{j}|\bigg)\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\leq\big\langle X_{\ell},\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X_{\ell})\big\rangle_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}.$
Proof.
The fact that  $\mathcal{L}^{*}(\mathcal{F}_{\ell})\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$  is easily verified using the definition of  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}$ . Therefore, considering the diagonal decomposition  $V_{k}=\sum_{\ell}V_{k,\ell}$  of the eigenvector  $V_{k}$  defined in Proposition 7, we find that if  $V_{k,\ell}\neq 0$ , then it is also an eigenvector of  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}$  with the same eigenvalue as that of  $V_{k}$ . On the other hand, by definition,  $V_{k}$  is a polynomial of degree  $k_{j}$  in terms of  $\mathbf{a}_{j}$  and  $\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}$ . This means that we have  $V_{k,\ell}=0$  if  $|\ell_{j}|>k_{j}$  for some  $j$ . We also note that since by Proposition 7, the closure of the span of  $V_{k}$ ’s is the whole space  $L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma})$ , the closure of the span of operators  $V_{k,\ell}$  equals  $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ . Indeed,  $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}=\overline{\text{span}\{V_{k,\ell}:\,k_{j}\geq|\ell_{j}|,\forall j\}}$ . Putting these together the desired result is implied.
∎
To state our next lemma it is convenient to extend the definition of the entropy function for operators that are not necessarily normalized. For any positive operator  $X=\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2}(\rho^{1/2})$  where  $\rho$  is a density operator, we define
$\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)=D(\rho\|\widehat{\sigma}).$
Extending this definition to non-normalized operators satisfying  $\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}<+\infty$ , we let
$\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)=\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}\,\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\Big(\frac{X}{\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}}\Big).$
The significance of this entropy function is in its connection to the derivative of  $p\mapsto\|X\|_{p,\widehat{\sigma}}$  at  $p=2$  for which we refer to [39, 35, 2].
Lemma 9.
Let  $X$  be a positive operator satisfying  $\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho H_{m}\big)<+\infty$  where  $\rho=\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{1/2}(X)^{2}$  and  $H_{m}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}$  is the  $m$ -mode number operator.
Then, for any vector  $w=(w_{\ell})_{\ell}$  of positive real numbers we have
$\displaystyle\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)\leq\sum_{\ell}\big(\log\|w\|_{2}^{2}-\log w_{\ell}^{2}\big)\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}+\sum_{\ell}\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\big(I_{2,2}(X_{\ell})\big),$
(41)
where  $X_{\ell}$ ’s are given by the diagonal decomposition  $X=\sum_{\ell}X_{\ell}$  with  $X_{\ell}\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ . Also,  $I_{2,2}(X_{\ell})=\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2}\big(\big|\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{1/2}(X_{\ell})\big|\big)$  and
$\|w\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{2}$ .
Proof.
Fix a finite subset  $S\subset\mathbb{Z}^{m}$  satisfying  $-\ell\in S$  for all  $\ell\in S$ . For some technical reason, in the following we restrict to the subspace of operators  $X$  satisfying  $X_{\ell}=0$  if  $\ell\notin S$ . Later, we will relax this assumption.
For any  $z\in\mathbb{C}$  define the map  $T_{z}$  by
$T_{z}(X)=\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{z}X_{\ell},$
where as before  $X=\sum_{\ell}X_{\ell}$  is the diagonal decomposition of  $X$ . Note that by the above assumption this sum is indeed a finite sum and over  $\ell\in S$ .
By the orthogonality of the subspaces  $\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$  for any  $t\in\mathbb{R}$  we have
$\displaystyle\big\|T_{it}(X)\big\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}=\Big\|\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{it}X_{\ell}\Big\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}=\sum_{\ell}|w_{\ell}^{it}|^{2}\cdot\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}=\sum_{\ell}\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}.$
(42)
Next, recall the definition of norm  $\|\cdot\|_{p,\widehat{\sigma}}$  given by (37). Using the triangle and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities, for any  $t\in\mathbb{R}$  we have
$\displaystyle\big\|T_{1+it}(X)\big\|_{\infty,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}$
$\displaystyle=\Big\|\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{1+it}X_{\ell}\Big\|_{\infty,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\Big(\sum_{\ell}|w_{\ell}^{1+it}|\cdot\|X_{k}\|_{\infty,\widehat{\sigma}}\Big)^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\Big(\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{\ell}\|X_{\ell}\|_{\infty,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}\Big).$
(43)
For any  $1\leq p\leq+\infty$  define
$\|X\|_{2,p,\widehat{\sigma}}:=\Big(\sum_{\ell}\|X_{\ell}\|^{2}_{p,\widehat{\sigma}}\Big)^{1/2}.$
It is well-known and can be easily verified that  $\|\cdot\|_{2,p,\widehat{\sigma}}$  satisfies the triangle inequality and is really a norm. Moreover, these norms form an interpolation family [40].
Now, with this notation, (42) and (43) imply that
$\|T_{it}\|_{(2,2,\widehat{\sigma})\to(2,\widehat{\sigma})}=1,\qquad\|T_{1+it}\|_{(2,\infty,\widehat{\sigma})\to(\infty,\widehat{\sigma})}\leq\|w\|_{2},\qquad\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R}.$
Therefore, by the interpolation inequality [37], we have
$\displaystyle\|T_{1-2/p}\|_{(2,p,\sigma)\to(p,\sigma)}\leq\|w\|_{2}^{1-2/p},\qquad\quad\forall~2\leq p\leq+\infty.$
This means that
$\displaystyle\Big\|\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{1-2/p}X_{\ell}\Big\|_{p}\leq\|w\|_{2}^{1-2/p}\cdot\Big(\sum_{\ell}\|X_{\ell}\|_{p}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}.$
We note that this inequality turns into an equality for  $p=2$ . Therefore, we must have
$\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}p}\bigg(\Big\|\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{1-2/p}X_{\ell}\Big\|_{p}\bigg)\bigg|_{p=2}\leq\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}p}\bigg(\|w\|_{2}^{1-2/p}\cdot\Big(\sum_{\ell}\|X_{\ell}\|_{p}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}\bigg)\bigg|_{p=2}.$
Computing the derivative of both sides by [2, Proposition 3] and using the fact that  $X_{\ell}^{\dagger}=X_{-\ell}$ , the desired inequality is obtained.
Now we relax the assumption that  $X_{\ell}$  is non-zero only for finitely many  $\ell$ . Assume that  $X=\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2}\big(\rho^{1/2}\big)$  where  $\rho$  is a quantum state with finite mean photon number, in which case
$\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)=\|X\|^{2}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}D(\rho\|\widehat{\sigma})=-\|X\|^{2}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\big(S(\rho)+\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\widehat{\sigma})\big).$
Let  $\Pi_{k}$  be the projection on the span of basis vectors  $|n_{1},\dots,n_{m}\rangle$  satisfying  $n_{1}+\cdots+n_{m}\leq k$ . Let  $X^{(k)}=\Pi_{k}X\Pi_{k}$  and consider the quantum state  $\rho^{(k)}=\|X^{(k)}\|^{-2}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2}\big(X^{(k)}\big)^{2}$ .
Observe that  $X_{\ell}^{(k)}$  is non-zero only for finitely many values of  $\ell$ . Then, by the above argument (41) holds for  $X^{(k)}$ . Taking the limit of  $k\to+\infty$ , clearly  $\big\|X_{\ell}^{(k)}\big\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}$  tends to  $\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}$ , which also implies that the  $2$ -norm of  $X^{(k)}$  tends to that of  $X$ . For the entropy terms, it can be verified that the mean photon number of  $\rho^{(k)}$  tends to that of  $\rho$ . This implies that  $\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{(k)}\log\widehat{\sigma}\big)$  tends to  $\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\widehat{\sigma})$ .
Next, using the assumption  $\text{\rm tr}(\rho H_{m})<+\infty$ , we can apply the continuity bound for the entropy function [43, Lemma 18] to conclude that  $S\big(\rho^{(k)}\big)$  tends to  $S(\rho)$ . Therefore,
$\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\big(X^{(k)}\big)\to\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)$  and similarly  $\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\big(I_{2,2}\big(X^{(k)}_{\ell}\big)\to\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\big(I_{2,2}(X_{\ell})$  as  $k\to+\infty$ . Putting these together the desired inequality for  $X$  is implied.
∎
We remark that Lemma 9 holds beyond the diagonal decomposition considered above and works for any decomposition of the space of operators into orthogonal subspaces. Thus, this lemma is of independent interest and may find other applications.
Theorem 10.
For any  $\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{m}>0$  we have
$\displaystyle\widehat{\alpha}_{2}\geq\bigg(\frac{2+\log(2m+1)}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2,\min}}\bigg)^{-1},$
where  $\beta_{\min}=\min_{j}\beta_{j}$  and  $\alpha_{2,\min}=\min_{j}\frac{4\sinh^{2}(\beta_{j}/4)}{\beta_{j}}=\frac{4\sinh^{2}(\beta_{\min}/4)}{\beta_{\min}}$ .
Proof.
We need to show that
$\displaystyle\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)\leq\bigg(\frac{2+\log(2m+1)}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2,\min}}\bigg)\big\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}},$
(44)
for any  $X$  satisfying  $\text{\rm tr}\big(\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{1/2}(X)^{2}H_{m}\big)<+\infty$ .
We use Lemma 9 for the choice of  $w_{\ell}=e^{-\frac{c}{2}|\ell|}$  where  $c>0$  and  $|\ell|=\sum_{j=1}^{m}|\ell_{j}|$ . We have  $\log\|w\|_{2}^{2}-\log w_{\ell}^{2}=c|\ell|+m\log\frac{e^{c}+1}{e^{c}-1}$  and
$\displaystyle\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)\leq m\log\frac{e^{c}+1}{e^{c}-1}\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}+c\sum_{\ell}|\ell|\cdot\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}+\sum_{\ell}\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(I_{2,2}(X_{\ell})).$
(45)
Now, since  $X_{\ell}\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ , by Corollary 8 we have
$\sum_{\ell}|\ell|\cdot\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}\sum_{\ell}\big\langle X_{\ell},\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X_{\ell})\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}=\frac{1}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}\big\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.$
Next, using the fact that  $X_{\ell}\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}$ , it is easily verified that the operator  $I_{2,2}(X_{\ell})$  is diagonal. On the other hand, the restriction of  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}$  to diagonal operators is essentially a classical Markov semigroup for which the tensorization property holds. Thus, the  $2$ -log-Sobolev constant of  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}$  restricted to diagonal operators equals the minimum of the  $2$ -log-Sobolev constants of  $\mathcal{L}^{*}_{j}$ ’s restricted to (single-mode) diagonal operators. The latter quantity is computed in Theorem 4. Putting these together we conclude that
$\alpha_{2,\min}\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(I_{2,2}(X_{\ell}))\leq\big\langle I_{2,2}(X_{\ell}),\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}\big(I_{2,2}(X_{\ell})\big)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.$
Using the above two inequalities in (45) we find that
$\displaystyle\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)$
$\displaystyle\leq m\log\frac{e^{c}+1}{e^{c}-1}\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}+\frac{c}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}\big\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2,\min}}\sum_{\ell}\big\langle I_{2}(X_{\ell}),\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}\big(I_{2}(X_{\ell})\big)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.$
It is shown in [2, Lemma 23] that for any operator  $Y$ ,
$\big\langle I_{2,2}(Y),\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(I_{2,2}(Y))\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}+\big\langle I_{2,2}(Y^{\dagger}),\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(I_{2,2}(Y^{\dagger}))\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}\leq\big\langle Y,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(Y)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}+\big\langle Y^{\dagger},\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(Y^{\dagger})\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.$
Therefore, using  $X_{\ell}^{\dagger}=X_{-\ell}$ , the above inequalities imply
$\displaystyle\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)$
$\displaystyle\leq m\log\frac{e^{c}+1}{e^{c}-1}\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}+\frac{c}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X)\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2,\min}}\sum_{\ell}\big\langle X_{\ell},\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X_{\ell})\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}$
$\displaystyle=m\log\frac{e^{c}+1}{e^{c}-1}\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}+\Big(\frac{c}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2,\min}}\Big)\big\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.$
Next, by Proposition 7 the generator  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}$  has the spectral gap  $\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)$ . Thus, by [39, Theorem 4.2] the above inequality implies
$\displaystyle\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)$
$\displaystyle\leq\bigg(\frac{1+m\log\frac{e^{c}+1}{e^{c}-1}}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}+\frac{c}{\sinh(\beta_{\min}/2)}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2,\min}}\bigg)\big\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.$
Finally, letting  $c=\log(2m+1)$  and using  $\log(1+\frac{1}{m})\leq\frac{1}{m}$  the desired inequality (44) is obtained.
∎
5 Proof of the CMOE conjecture
In this section, we present an alternative proof of the CMOE conjecture for single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels, which is first established in [15, 16].
Theorem 11.
[CMOE Conjecture]
For any single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channel  $\Phi$ , and any quantum state  $\rho$  with finite mean photon number we have
$\displaystyle S\big(\Phi(\rho)\big)\geq S\big(\Phi(\tau)\big),$
(46)
where  $\tau$  is a single-mode thermal state satisfying  $S(\rho)=S(\tau)$ .
To prove this theorem we first state a consequence of Theorem 1.
Theorem 12.
Let  $\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\}$  denote a semigroup of single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels. Then, for any  $\alpha>0$  we have
$\displaystyle\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(\alpha)=\inf_{\rho}\,\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}S\big(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\big)\Big|_{t=0}+\alpha S(\rho),$
(47)
where the infimum is taken over all quantum states  $\rho$  with finite mean photon number, and  $\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(\alpha)$  is the infimum of the same function restricted to thermal states.
Proof of Theorem 12.
Let  $\mathcal{L}$  be the Lindbladian of the semigroup  $\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\}$  so that  $\Phi_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}}$ . We have
$\displaystyle\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}S\big(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\big)\Big|_{t=0}=\langle\mathcal{L}(\rho),\log\rho\rangle.$
(48)
Then, the claim follows from Theorem 1 for  $p=1$  and appropriate choices of  $\nu_{0},\nu_{1}\geq 0$  and  $\omega=0$ .
∎
We need yet another technical ingredient to prove Theorem 11. For  $0<x<1$  let
$\displaystyle\tau_{x}=(1-x)\sum_{n}x^{n}|n\rangle\langle n|,$
(49)
be a thermal state with parameter  $x$ . Then, letting  $\Phi_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}}$  with  $\mathcal{L}=\nu_{0}\mathcal{L}_{0}+\nu_{1}\mathcal{L}_{1}$  and using (48), we find that the objective function in (47) for thermal states equals
$\displaystyle f_{\alpha}(x)$
$\displaystyle:=\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}S\big(\Phi_{t}(\tau_{x})\big)\big|_{t=0}+\alpha S(\tau_{x})$
$\displaystyle\,=\frac{1}{1-x}\Big(\!(\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0})\log x-\alpha x\log x-\alpha(1-x)\log(1-x)\!\Big).$
This equation can also be derived by taking the limit of  $p\to 1^{+}$  in (18).
Assume that  $\nu_{0}>0$  and as before let  $\alpha>0$ . Then, we have  $\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}f_{\alpha}(x)=\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}f_{\alpha}(x)=+\infty$ . This means that the minimum of  $f_{\alpha}(x)$  is attained at roots of  $f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x)$ . We have
$\displaystyle f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-x}\Big(\nu_{1}\log x+\frac{\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0}}{x}-\alpha\log x+\alpha\log(1-x)\Big)$
$\displaystyle\quad~+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\Big((\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0})\log x-\alpha x\log x-\alpha(1-x)\log(1-x)\Big)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\bigg(\!(\nu_{1}-\nu_{0})\log x+\frac{(1-x)(\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0})}{x}-\alpha\log x\bigg)$
Therefore,  $f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x)=0$  iff  $g(x)=\alpha$  where
$g(x):=\nu_{1}-\nu_{0}+\frac{(1-x)(\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0})}{x\log x}.$
Computing the derivative of  $g(x)$ , we have
$g^{\prime}(x)=\frac{\nu_{0}(\log x-x+1)+\nu_{1}(x(x-1)-x^{2}\log x)}{x^{2}\log^{2}x}.$
Then, using  $\log x\leq x-1$  and  $-\log x=\log\frac{1}{x}\leq\frac{1}{x}-1$  we find that  $g^{\prime}(x)\leq 0$  for  $0<x<1$ , and that  $g(x)$  is monotone decreasing in this interval. Moreover, since  $\nu_{0}>0$  we have  $\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}g(x)=+\infty$  and  $\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}g(x)=0$ . This means that  $g(x)\geq 0$  for all  $0<x<1$ , and  $g(x)$  takes any positive value in this interval exactly once.
As a conclusion,  $g(x)=\alpha$  has exactly one solution in  $(0,1)$  for any  $\alpha>0$ . We conclude that, if  $\alpha>0$ , the minimum of  $f_{\alpha}(x)$  is attained at the unique root of  $f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x)$ . More importantly, for any  $0<x_{0}<1$ , there is  $\alpha_{0}=g(x_{0})$  such that the minimum of  $f_{\alpha_{0}}(x)$  is attained at  $x=x_{0}$ .
Proof of Theorem 11.
As a phase-covariant Gaussian channel, we have  $\Phi=\Phi_{t_{1}}$  for some phase-covariant Gaussian semigroup  $\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\}$  and some  $t_{1}>0$ .1313
13
If  $t_{1}=0$ , then  $\Phi$  is the identity channel and there is nothing to prove. Let  $\mathcal{L}=\nu_{0}\mathcal{L}_{0}+\nu_{1}\mathcal{L}_{1}$  be the Lindbladian of this semigroup. In order to apply the above computations, by taking the limit of  $\nu_{0}\to 0^{+}$  we assume with no loss of generality that  $\nu_{0}>0$ . The point is that if  $S\big(\Phi_{t_{1}}(\rho)\big)\geq S(\Phi_{t_{1}}(\tau))$  holds for any  $\nu_{0}>0$ , then by the continuity of von Neumann entropy [43, Lemma 18], it holds for  $\nu_{0}=0$  as well.
Suppose that  $S\big(\Phi_{t_{1}}(\rho)\big)<S(\Phi_{t_{1}}(\tau_{x_{0}}))$  where  $\tau=\tau_{x_{0}}$  is the thermal state in the statement of the theorem with parameter  $x_{0}$  as in (49). We note that by assumption  $S(\Phi_{t}(\rho))=S(\Phi_{t}(\tau_{x_{0}}))$  for  $t=0$ . Thus, we may define
$t_{0}=\sup\big\{t:\,S\big(\Phi_{t}^{\otimes m}(\rho)\big)\geq mS\big(\Phi_{t}(\tau_{x_{0}})\big),t<t_{1}\big\}.$
Then, by continuity we have  $S(\Phi_{t_{0}}(\rho))=S(\Phi_{t_{0}}(\tau_{x_{0}}))$  and
$\displaystyle S(\Phi_{t}(\rho))<S(\Phi_{t}(\tau_{x_{0}})),\qquad\forall t_{0}<t\leq t_{1}.$
(50)
Recall that  $\Phi_{t}(\tau_{x_{0}})$  is a thermal state for any  $t>0$ . Let  $x_{t}$  be the parameter of this thermal state:  $\tau_{x_{t}}=\Phi_{t}(\tau_{x_{0}})$ . We note that  $t\mapsto x_{t}$  is smooth. Then, by the above discussions, there is a smooth function  $t\mapsto\alpha_{t}$  with  $\alpha_{t}>0$  such that
$\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(\alpha_{t})=\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}s}S\big(\Phi_{s}(\tau_{x_{t}})\big)\big|_{s=0}+\alpha_{t}S(\tau_{x_{t}}).$
Employing Theorem 12, for any  $t_{0}\leq t\leq t_{1}$  we obtain
$\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}S\big(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\big)+\alpha_{t}S(\Phi_{t}(\rho))\geq\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}S(\tau_{x_{t}})+\alpha_{t}S(\tau_{x_{t}}).$
Taking the integral of both sides yields
$\displaystyle S\big(\Phi_{t_{1}}(\rho)\big)-S\big(\Phi_{t_{0}}(\rho)\big)+\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\!\alpha_{t}S(\Phi_{t}(\rho))\,\text{\rm{d}}t\geq S(\tau_{x_{t_{1}}})-S(\tau_{x_{t_{0}}})+\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\!\alpha_{t}S(\tau_{x_{t}})\,\text{\rm{d}}t.$
We note that  $S(\Phi_{t_{0}}(\rho))=S(\tau_{x_{t_{0}}})$ , so this inequality is in contradiction with (50). This implies that the starting inequality  $S\big(\Phi_{t_{1}}(\rho)\big)<S(\Phi_{t_{1}}(\tau_{x_{0}}))$  does not hold.
∎
Generalization of the CMOE conjecture to the multimode case is an open problem in general. However, generalizing the proof idea of Theorem 11 and using Theorem 3, we can prove the conjecture for a special class of multimode states that can be prepared by applying a passive Gaussian unitary  $U_{G}$  on an arbitrary product state,  $\rho=U_{G}\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_{m}U_{G}^{\dagger}$ .
6 Conclusion
In this paper, we introduced a meta log-Sobolev inequality, formalized by Theorem 1, that provides a general information theoretic framework to study phase-covariant Gaussian quantum channels. In general, this inequality and our technical proof, particularly the tensorization argument that we used in the second step, are of independent interest. However, by using this result, we have derived new optimal bounds in the context of  $p$ -log-Sobolev inequalities for the semigroup of attenuation channels.
Specifically, in Theorem 4, we explicitly computed the optimal  $p$ -log-Sobolev constant of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup for any  $1\leq p\leq 2$ . We also in Theorem 10 established a bound on the  $2$ -log-Sobolev constant in the multimode case that scales logarithmically with the number of modes. We conjecture that the log-Sobolev constants in the multimode case match those of the single-mode case and the tensorization property holds in general. We showed in Corollary 6 that this conjecture holds assuming that the optimal multimode states are Gaussian.
Quantum log-Sobolev inequalities are also defined for  $0\leq p<1$  and are related to reverse hypercontractivity inequalities [10, 2]. An interesting open problem is to compute the  $p$ -log-Sobolev constant for this range of parameter, which we leave it for future works.
The proof of our multimode log-Sobolev inequality is based on an entropic inequality in Lemma 9 which is of independent interest. Using this inequality, one might be able to prove log-Sobolev inequalities for the tensor product of other quantum Markov semigroups. We leave exploration of such applications of Lemma 9 for future works.
Our results have novel consequences even in the fully classical case, i.e., when restricting to states  $\rho$  that are diagonal in the Fock basis. In particular, as pointed out in [6], restricting the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup to diagonal states, we obtain a classical birth-death process whose log-Sobolev constants were not known prior to our work (except in the case of  $p=1$ ). Moreover, our results have consequences for the classical operation of thinning on the space of integer-valued random variables, for which we refer to [18] and references therein.
We also presented an alternative proof of the CMOE conjecture in Theorem 11 in the single-mode case. This conjecture in the multimode case is left as a major open problem.
Our results contribute to the resolution of Gaussian optimizer conjectures in the quantum case [18]. These conjectures state the optimality of Gaussian states for certain optimization problems regarding Gaussian channels. Theorem 1 establishes this conjecture for the quite general function  $\Upsilon(\rho)$  in the single-mode case. Generalizing this theorem for multimode states can resolve the CMOE conjecture in the multimode case. To this end, ideas developed in [19] might be useful. We leave further exploration of this problem for future works.

Appendix A Generators of phase-covariant Gaussian channels
In this appendix we show that any single-mode phase-covariant channel given by (11) is a member of a semigroup whose Lindbladian equals (12).
Let us consider the family of channels  $\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\}$  corresponding to parameters  $\{(\lambda_{t},\gamma_{t}):\,t\geq 0\}$  in (11):
$\chi_{\Phi_{t}(\rho)}(\xi)=\exp\!\bigg(\!\!-\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{t}|\xi|^{2}\bigg)\chi_{\rho}\big(\!\sqrt{\lambda_{t}}\,\xi\big).$
(51)
Suppose that  $\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\}$  is a semigroup which in particular means that  $\Phi_{0}$  is the identity channel corresponding to parameters  $\gamma_{0}=0$  and  $\lambda_{0}=1$ . Then, the generator of this semigroup is determined by
$\chi_{\mathcal{L}(\rho)}(\xi)=-\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}\chi_{\Phi_{t}(\rho)}(\xi)\Big|_{t=0}.$
Using (51) we compute the derivative
$\displaystyle\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}\chi_{\Phi_{t}(\rho)}(\xi)\Big|_{t=0}$
$\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\gamma^{\prime}_{0}\,|\xi|^{2}\text{\rm tr}(\rho D_{\xi})+\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\,\Big(\xi\,\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}D_{\xi}\big)-\bar{\xi}\,\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\,\mathbf{a}D_{\xi}\big)\Big)$
$\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{0}^{\prime}\,\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\big[\mathbf{a},[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},D_{\xi}]\big]\big)+\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{0}^{\prime}\Big(\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big[\mathbf{a},D_{\xi}\big]\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\,\mathbf{a}\big[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},D_{\xi}\big]\big)\Big)$
$\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{0}^{\prime}\,\text{\rm tr}\big(\big[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},[\mathbf{a},\rho]\big]D_{\xi}\big)+\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\Big(\text{\rm tr}\big(\big[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\,\mathbf{a}\big]D_{\xi}-\big[\mathbf{a},\rho\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big]D_{\xi}\big)\Big)$
$\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\gamma^{\prime}_{0}\,\chi_{[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},[\mathbf{a},\rho]]}(\xi)+\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\,\chi_{[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\mathbf{a}]-[\mathbf{a},\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}]}(\xi),$
where  $\lambda^{\prime}_{0}=\frac{\text{\rm{d}}\lambda_{t}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}\big|_{t=0}$ ,  $\gamma^{\prime}_{0}=\frac{\text{\rm{d}}\gamma_{t}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}\big|_{t=0}$ . Here, we use  $\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}\lambda}D_{\lambda\delta}=(\xi\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}-\bar{\xi}\mathbf{a})D_{\lambda\xi}$  in the first line, and the well-known equations
$[\mathbf{a},D_{\xi}]=\xi D_{\xi}$  and  $[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},D_{\xi}]=\bar{\xi}D_{\xi}$  in the second line. Replacing the characteristic functions in the above equation by their corresponding operators yields
$\displaystyle\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}\Phi_{t}(\rho)\Big|_{t=0}=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\gamma^{\prime}_{0}\,\big[\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},[\mathbf{a},\rho]\big]+\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\Big([\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\,\mathbf{a}]-[\mathbf{a},\rho\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}]\Big)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{0}^{\prime}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},\rho\big\}+\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\big\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho\,\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}\,\rho\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big)$
$\displaystyle\,+\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},\rho\big\}-\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\big\}+\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho\,\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}\,\rho\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\big(\gamma^{\prime}_{0}+\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\big)\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\big\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho\mathbf{a}\Big)-\frac{1}{2}\big(\gamma^{\prime}_{0}-\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\big)\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},\rho\big\}-\mathbf{a}\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big)$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\big(\gamma^{\prime}_{0}+\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\big)\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)-\frac{1}{2}\big(\gamma^{\prime}_{0}-\lambda^{\prime}_{0}\big)\mathcal{L}_{1}(\rho),$
where we define
$\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)=\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\big\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho\mathbf{a}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{L}_{1}(\rho)=\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},\rho\big\}-\mathbf{a}\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}.$
Therefore, if the channels defined by (51) form a semigroup, then the corresponding Lindbladian is equal to
$\mathcal{L}(\rho)=\frac{1}{2}\big(\gamma_{0}^{\prime}+\lambda_{0}^{\prime}\big)\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)+\frac{1}{2}\big(\gamma_{0}^{\prime}-\lambda_{0}^{\prime}\big)\mathcal{L}_{1}(\rho).$
(52)
We use this equation to obtain the generator of the three classes of phase-covariant Gaussian channels.
A.1 Attenuator channels
The attenuator channel can be physically modeled by overlapping the input state and a thermal state  $\sigma_{\beta}$  on a beam splitter with transmissivity  $\lambda$ :
$\Phi^{\text{att}}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\text{\rm tr}_{2}\Big(U_{\text{BS},\lambda}(\rho\otimes\sigma_{\beta})U_{\text{BS},\lambda}^{\dagger}\Big),$
where the 2-mode unitary operator  $U_{\text{BS},\lambda}$  can be described by
$\displaystyle\begin{cases}U_{BS,\lambda}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{1}U_{BS,\lambda}&=\sqrt{\lambda}\,\mathbf{a}_{1}+\sqrt{1-{\lambda}}\,\mathbf{a}_{2},\\
U_{BS,\lambda}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{2}U_{BS,\lambda}&=-\sqrt{1-{\lambda}}\,\mathbf{a}_{1}+\sqrt{\lambda}\,\mathbf{a}_{2}.\end{cases}$
(53)
Using these relations, the characteristic function of the two-mode state  $U_{\text{BS},\lambda}(\rho\otimes\sigma_{\beta})U_{\text{BS},\lambda}^{\dagger}$  equals
$\displaystyle\text{\rm tr}\Big(U_{\text{BS},\lambda}(\rho\otimes\sigma_{\beta})U_{\text{BS},\lambda}^{\dagger}D_{\xi_{1}}\otimes D_{\xi_{2}}\Big)$
$\displaystyle=\text{\rm tr}\Big(\rho\otimes\sigma_{\beta}U_{\text{BS},\lambda}^{\dagger}(D_{\xi_{1}}\otimes D_{\xi_{2}})U_{\text{BS},\lambda}\Big)$
$\displaystyle=\text{\rm tr}\Big(\!\rho D_{\sqrt{\lambda}\xi_{1}-\sqrt{1-{\lambda}}\xi_{2}}\Big)\,\text{\rm tr}\Big(\!\sigma_{\beta}D_{\sqrt{1-{\lambda}}\xi_{1}+\sqrt{\lambda}\xi_{2}}\Big).$
Thus, the characteristic function of the output state of the attenuation channel is given by
$\displaystyle\chi_{\Phi^{\text{att}}_{\lambda}(\rho)}(\xi)$
$\displaystyle=\chi_{\rho}\big(\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi_{1}-\sqrt{1-{\lambda}}\,\xi_{2}\big)\,\chi_{\sigma_{\beta}}\big(\sqrt{1-{\lambda}}\,\xi_{1}+\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi_{2}\big)\Big|_{(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=(\xi,0)}$
$\displaystyle=\chi_{\rho}\big(\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi\big)\,\chi_{\sigma_{\beta}}\big(\sqrt{1-{\lambda}}\,\xi\big)$
$\displaystyle=\exp\!\Big({\!{-\frac{1}{2}\coth(\beta/2)(1-\lambda)|\xi|^{2}}}\Big)\chi_{\rho}\big(\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi\big),$
where we replace the characteristic function of the thermal state from (9).
Setting  $\lambda=\lambda_{t}=e^{-2ct}$  with  $c>0$  in the above relation, we observe that attenuator channels  $\{\Phi^{\text{att}}_{\lambda_{t}}:\,t\geq 0\}$  form a semigroup. Comparing the above equation with (51) also gives  $\gamma_{t}=\coth(\beta/2)(1-\lambda_{t})$ . Therefore, by plugging  $\lambda_{0}^{\prime}=-2c$  and  $\gamma_{0}^{\prime}=2c\coth(\beta/2)$  into (52), we obtain the corresponding generator
$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\rho)$
$\displaystyle=c\big(\!\coth(\beta/2)-1\big)\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)+c\big(\!\coth(\beta/2)+1\big)\mathcal{L}_{1}(\rho).$
A.2 Amplifier channels
Following a similar procedure as for attenuator channels, we can derive the generator of the semigroup of amplifier channels. An amplifier channel can be modeled by applying a two-mode squeezing unitary with squeezing parameter  $\lambda\geq 1$  on the input state and a thermal state  $\sigma_{\beta}$ , and then tracing over the second mode:
$\Phi^{\text{amp}}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\text{\rm tr}_{2}\Big(U_{\text{2S},\lambda}(\rho\otimes\sigma_{\beta})U_{\text{2S},\lambda}^{\dagger}\Big).$
Here, the action of the two-mode squeezing unitary can be described by
$\displaystyle\begin{cases}U_{2S,\lambda}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{1}U_{2S,\lambda}&=\sqrt{\lambda}\,\mathbf{a}_{1}+\sqrt{{\lambda}-2}\,\mathbf{a}_{2}^{\dagger},\\
U_{2S,\lambda}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{2}U_{2S,\lambda}&=\sqrt{\lambda}\,\mathbf{a}_{2}+\sqrt{{\lambda}-1}\,\mathbf{a}_{1}^{\dagger}.\end{cases}$
(54)
Using these relations, we have
$U_{2S,\lambda}^{\dagger}D_{\xi_{1}}\otimes D_{\xi_{2}}U_{2S,\lambda}=D_{\xi_{1}\sqrt{\lambda}-\bar{\xi}_{2}\sqrt{\lambda-1}}\otimes D_{\xi_{2}\sqrt{\lambda}-\bar{\xi}_{1}\sqrt{\lambda-1}}.$
Thus, the characteristic function of the output state is given by
$\displaystyle\chi_{\Phi^{\text{amp}}_{\lambda}(\rho)}(\xi)$
$\displaystyle=\chi_{\rho}\big(\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi_{1}-\sqrt{\lambda-1}\,\bar{\xi}_{2}\big)\,\chi_{\sigma_{\beta}}\big(\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi_{2}-\sqrt{\lambda-1}\,\bar{\xi}_{1}\big)\Big|_{(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=(\xi,0)}$
$\displaystyle=\chi_{\rho}\big(\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi\big)\,\chi_{\sigma_{\beta}}\big(\sqrt{{\lambda}-1}\,\xi\big)$
$\displaystyle=\exp\!\Big(\!{{-\frac{1}{2}\coth(\beta/2)(\lambda-1)|\xi|^{2}}}\Big)\chi_{\rho}\big(\sqrt{\lambda}\,\xi\big),$
where in the last line the characteristic function of the thermal state (9) is replaced.
Setting  $\lambda=\lambda_{t}=e^{2ct}$  with  $c>0$ , we observe that amplifier channels  $\{\Phi^{\text{amp}}_{\lambda_{t}}:\,t\geq 0\}$  form a semigroup. Here,  $\gamma_{t}=\coth(\beta/2)(\lambda_{t}-1)$ . Thus, by plugging  $\lambda_{0}^{\prime}=2c$  and  $\gamma_{0}^{\prime}=2c\coth(\beta/2)$  in (52), we obtain the generator
$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\rho)$
$\displaystyle=c\big(\!\coth(\beta/2)+1\big)\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)+c\big(\!\coth(\beta/2)-1\big)\mathcal{L}_{1}(\rho).$
Note that here we get the same coefficients as those of the generator of the attenuator semigroup, but swapped.
A.3 Additive-noise channels
The classical additive-noise Gaussian channels can be modeled by applying a displacement operator whose parameter is chosen at random according to a Gaussian probability distribution:
$\Phi^{\text{add}}_{\gamma}(\rho)=\frac{2}{\pi\gamma}\int e^{-\frac{2}{\gamma}|\alpha|^{2}}D_{\alpha}\rho D^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\,\text{\rm{d}}^{2}\alpha.$
The characteristic function of the output state of this channel is given by
$\displaystyle\chi_{\Phi^{\text{add}}_{\gamma}(\rho)}(\xi)$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{\pi\gamma}\int e^{-\frac{2}{\gamma}|\alpha|^{2}}\text{\rm tr}\big(D_{\alpha}\rho D^{\dagger}_{\alpha}D_{\xi}\big)\,\text{\rm{d}}^{2}\alpha$
$\displaystyle=\frac{2}{\pi\gamma}\chi_{\rho}(\xi)\int e^{-\frac{2}{\gamma}|\alpha|^{2}}e^{\xi\bar{\alpha}-\bar{\xi}\alpha}\,\text{\rm{d}}^{2}\alpha$
$\displaystyle=\exp\!\Big({-\frac{1}{2}\gamma|\xi|^{2}}\Big)\chi_{\rho}(\xi),$
where we use  $D^{\dagger}_{\alpha}D_{\xi}D_{\alpha}=\exp(\xi\bar{\alpha}-\bar{\xi}\alpha)D_{\xi}$  in the second line.
By choosing  $\gamma=2ct$  with  $c>0$ , the channels  $\{\Phi^{\text{add}}_{t}:\,t\geq 0\}$  form a semigroup. Here,  $\lambda_{t}=1$ . Thus, by inserting  $\lambda_{0}^{\prime}=0$  and  $\gamma_{0}^{\prime}=2c$  in (52) we obtain the generator
$\mathcal{L}(\rho)=c\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)+c\mathcal{L}_{1}(\rho).$
Appendix B  $\Upsilon(\rho)$  is well-defined if  $\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a})<+\infty$
In this appendix we show that  $\Upsilon(\rho)$  given by
$\displaystyle\Upsilon(\rho)=\hat{p}\bigg(\!\nu_{0}\Big[\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\Big]+\nu_{1}\Big[\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}\big)\!\Big]\!\bigg)+\omega\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big)+S(\rho).$
is well-defined for any state  $\rho$  with finite mean photon number. For such a state both  $\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}),\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger})$  are finite. Moreover, if  $\rho=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}|\psi_{j}\rangle\langle\psi_{j}|$  is the eigen-decomposition of  $\rho$ , then we have
$\displaystyle\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{i}^{1/p}\lambda_{j}^{1/\hat{p}}\big|\langle\psi_{i}|\mathbf{a}|\psi_{j}\rangle\big|^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i,j}\Big(\frac{1}{p}\lambda_{i}+\frac{1}{\hat{p}}\lambda_{j}\Big)\big|\langle\psi_{i}|\mathbf{a}|\psi_{j}\rangle\big|^{2}$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{p}\lambda_{i}\big\|\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}|\psi_{i}\rangle\big\|^{2}+\sum_{j}\frac{1}{\hat{p}}\lambda_{j}\big\|\mathbf{a}|\psi_{j}\rangle\big\|^{2}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p}\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)+\frac{1}{\hat{p}}\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big),$
where in the second line we use Young’s inequality. Thus,  $\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)$  and similarly  $\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}\big)$  are finite. Also, using the non-negativity of Umegaki’s quantum relative entropy  $D(\rho\|\tau)=\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\tau)$ , for the thermal state  $\tau=(1-1/e)e^{-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}}$  we have
$\displaystyle 0\leq D(\rho\|\tau)=-S(\rho)-\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\tau)=-S(\rho)-\log(1-1/e)+\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big).$
Therefore, since  $\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big)$  is finite,  $S(\rho)$  is also finite.
Appendix C Verification of (36)
Recall that
$\displaystyle\phi(x,y)=$
$\displaystyle-y^{2}\log y^{2}-(1-y^{2})\log(1-y^{2})+y^{2}\log x^{2}+(1-y^{2})\log(1-x^{2})$
$\displaystyle\,-\frac{\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\log x^{2}}{\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}.$
Then, computing the derivative term-by-term yields
$\displaystyle\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}x}\phi(x,y)=$
$\displaystyle\frac{2y^{2}}{x}-\frac{2x(1-y^{2})}{1-x^{2}}-\frac{2\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}{x\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}$
$\displaystyle\,-\frac{2x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\log x^{2}}{px\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}-\frac{2x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\log x^{2}}{\hat{p}x\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}$
$\displaystyle\,-\frac{2x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}\big)\log x^{2}}{px\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)^{2}\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}-\frac{2x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\log x^{2}}{\hat{p}x\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)^{2}}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{2(x^{2}-y^{2})}{x(1-x^{2})}-\frac{2\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}{x\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}$
$\displaystyle\,-\frac{2x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\log x^{2}}{px\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)^{2}\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}-\frac{2x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\log x^{2}}{\hat{p}x\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)^{2}}.$
Therefore, we have
$\displaystyle\frac{x}{2}\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}x}$
$\displaystyle\phi(x,y)+\frac{x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}{\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}\bigg[\frac{\log x^{2}}{p(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}})}+1\bigg]+\frac{x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)}{\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}\bigg[\frac{\log x^{2}}{\hat{p}(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}})}+1\bigg]$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{(x^{2}-y^{2})}{(1-x^{2})}-\frac{\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)}{\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle-\frac{(x^{2}-y^{2})}{(1-x^{2})}+\frac{x^{2}-y^{2}+x^{\frac{2}{p}}y^{2}-x^{2}y^{\frac{2}{p}}+x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}y^{2}-x^{2}y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}}{\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{-(x^{2}-y^{2})\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)+\big(1-x^{2}\big)\big(x^{2}-y^{2}+x^{\frac{2}{p}}y^{2}-x^{2}y^{\frac{2}{p}}+x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}y^{2}-x^{2}y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}{\big(1-x^{2}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}$
$\displaystyle=$
$\displaystyle\frac{x^{2}\Big(\!\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{p}}-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)+\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-y^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}-y^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)\!\Big)}{\big(1-x^{2}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{p}}\big)\big(1-x^{\frac{2}{\hat{p}}}\big)}.$
This gives (36).
Appendix D Proof of  $\alpha_{2}=\min_{p\geq 1}\alpha_{p}$
In this appendix, we show that for any  $p\geq 1$  the following inequality holds:
$\displaystyle\frac{p\hat{p}}{4}\big(1-e^{-\beta/p}\big)\big(1-e^{-\beta/\hat{p}}\big)\geq\big(1-e^{-\beta/2}\big)^{2}.$
First, we may restrict to  $p\in[1,2]$ . Then, with the change of variable  $p=\frac{2}{1+t}$  with  $t\in[0,1]$  the above inequality is equivalent to
$\displaystyle\big(1-e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(1+t)}\big)\big(1-e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(1-t)}\big)\geq(1-t^{2})\big(1-e^{-\beta/2}\big)^{2}.$
Starting with the left hand side we compute
$\displaystyle\big(1-e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(1+t)}\big)\big(1-e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(1-t)}\big)$
$\displaystyle=1+e^{-\beta}-e^{-\beta/2}\big(e^{\beta t/2}+e^{-\beta t/2}\big)$
$\displaystyle=1+e^{-\beta}-2e^{-\beta/2}\sum_{k:\text{ even}}\frac{1}{k!}\Big(\frac{\beta t}{2}\Big)^{k}$
$\displaystyle\geq 1+e^{-\beta}-2e^{-\beta/2}\bigg(1+t^{2}\sum_{k\geq 2:\text{ even}}\frac{1}{k!}\Big(\frac{\beta}{2}\Big)^{k}\bigg)$
$\displaystyle=\big(1-e^{-\beta/2}\big)^{2}-t^{2}e^{-\beta/2}\Big(e^{\beta/2}+e^{-\beta/2}-2\Big)$
$\displaystyle=(1-t^{2})\big(1-e^{-\beta/2}\big)^{2}.$
Here, the inequality holds since  $0\leq t\leq 1$ . We are done.
Appendix E Proof of Proposition 7
It suffices to prove the proposition for  $m=1$ . In this case, we drop subscript  $j$  and denote  $\widehat{\mathcal{L}}$  and  $\widehat{\sigma}$  simply by  $\mathcal{L}$  and  $\sigma$ , respectively.
Using the commutation relation  $[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}]=1$ , we find that  $[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{q}_{z}]=\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}$ , and
$\big[\mathbf{a},e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}\big]=\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\Big(\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}e^{st-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}\Big)\Big|_{t=\mathbf{q}_{z}}=\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}se^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}.$
This means that
$e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}\mathbf{a}=\Big(\mathbf{a}-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}s\Big)e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}},$
and similarly
$e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}=\Big(\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}+\frac{\bar{z}}{\sqrt{2}}s\Big)e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}.$
Using these and  $|z|=1$ , a straightforward computation shows that
$\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{*}(e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}})$
$\displaystyle=e^{\beta/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}+\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}+\frac{\bar{z}}{\sqrt{2}}s)(\mathbf{a}-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}s)-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{a}-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}s)\Big)e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}$
$\displaystyle\quad\,+e^{-\beta/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}+\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a}-\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}s)(\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}+\frac{\bar{z}}{\sqrt{2}}s)-\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}+\frac{\bar{z}}{\sqrt{2}}s)\Big)e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}$
$\displaystyle=e^{\beta/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{1}{4}s^{2}\Big)e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}+e^{-\beta/2}\Big(-\frac{1}{2}s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{1}{4}s^{2}\Big)e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{e^{\beta/2}-e^{-\beta/2}}{2}s\Big(\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{2}s\Big)e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\coth(\beta/2)}{4}s^{2}}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{e^{\beta/2}-e^{-\beta/2}}{2}s\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}s}e^{s\mathbf{q}_{z}-\frac{\nu}{4}s^{2}}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{e^{\beta/2}-e^{-\beta/2}}{2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{s^{k}}{(k-1)!}h_{n}(\mathbf{q}_{z}).$
Comparing to (39) we find that
$\mathcal{L}^{*}\big(h_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{z})\big)=\big(\sinh(\beta/2)k\big)\,h_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{z}).$
Finally, note that the operators  $h_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{z})$ , over all  $k\geq 0$  and  $|z|=1$ , span the whole space of polynomials of  $\mathbf{a}$  and  $\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}$ , which is dense in  $L_{2}(\sigma)$ .
